sources.headline: Xi’s Gang of Three
sources.text:
As the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) prepares to convene the Fifth Plenum of its 20th Central Committee, rumors about personnel changes at the top are once again sweeping through overseas Chinese-language circles. One of the most outlandish claims is that Premier Li Qiang, the formal second-in-command, has already been designated as Xi Jinping’s successor and will even replace him as party general secretary at the upcoming meeting. Before last year’s Fourth Plenum, it was Cai Qi, another member of the Politburo Standing Committee, who was rumored to be Xi’s successor.
Neither claim is credible. Yet taken together, these rumors inadvertently reveal something fundamental about the workings of Chinese elite politics: Xi relies heavily on Li and Cai, his two most important lieutenants, to sustain his rule.
Understanding Chinese elite politics requires identifying the relationships that determine how power operates, rather than obsessing over supposed clues in every meeting or photograph. One reason outside observers have repeatedly misjudged Xi’s rule is that they have become lost in the fog of power struggles, imagining Zhongnanhai, the Chinese leadership compound, as a place perpetually on the verge of a palace coup while overlooking how the system functions on a daily basis.
However much power Xi has concentrated in his own hands, he cannot personally manage the enormous machinery of the Chinese state, or the vast CCP itself. He needs lieutenants. Within the 20th Politburo, Li and Cai are his two most indispensable aides—one overseeing government affairs, the other party affairs. Together, they constitute what I call the “central gang of three” that defines elite politics in the Xi era.
By “gang of three,” I don’t mean to suggest that the three constitute a faction akin to the notorious Gang of Four of the Cultural Revolution (1966-76), the gaggle of revolutionary leaders who were later blamed for the disasters of the period. Rather, this is a framework for understanding power. Zhou Enlai, the first premier of the People’s Republic of China, once advised senior military commanders newly entering the highest levels of politics that understanding the political situation required grasping and navigating what he called “central politics”—the relationships among Mao Zedong, military leader Lin Biao, and Mao’s wife, Jiang Qing, the three-most powerful figures at the time.
Zhou’s observation captured the essence of elite politics during the Cultural Revolution. Mao occupied the center, while Lin and Jiang drew on different sources of political power to secure their exceptional positions. Both depended on Mao, yet they also competed with each other. Lin would lose out in 1971, when a still mysterious set of events resulted in his death. Jiang would fall in 1976, when the Gang of Four, which she headed, was toppled by Mao’s successor, Hua Guofeng.
Today, Xi, Li, and Cai form a similarly unequal triangle: Xi is the supreme authority over both men, while Li and Cai perform distinct functions, share common interests, and remain potential competitors.
But the historical similarities should not obscure the more important differences. Lin was not only Mao’s officially designated successor but also a military commander with wartime achievements, considerable prestige, and long-standing connections within the armed forces. Jiang enjoyed the unique status of being Mao’s wife, along with the political network she built during the Cultural Revolution. Neither could have exercised power without Mao, but neither depended entirely on his day-to-day authorization—particularly Lin.
Li and Cai are different. Both owe their political ascent to the trust they established with Xi during their careers in provincial and central government. Neither possesses the independent political capital that Lin commanded, much less the familial connection that gave Jiang her special standing. As a result, the interests binding Xi, Li, and Cai are more closely aligned than those that bound Mao, Lin, and Jiang, and neither man can establish independent centers of power outside Xi’s authority.
Xi has clearly divided responsibilities between Li and Cai while preventing either from monopolizing power within his respective domain. Xi relies on both without publicly showing a pronounced preference for either. At least so far, there is no visible evidence of the kind of acute, overt conflict that characterized relations between Lin and Jiang.
The division of responsibilities between Li and Cai since the 20th Party Congress in 2022 appears straightforward. Li serves as premier of the State Council and ranks second in the party hierarchy. Cai, meanwhile, is the highest-ranking secretary of the Secretariat, the Politburo’s executive arm. Although he ranks fifth in the party hierarchy, Cai oversees the Secretariat’s daily work and simultaneously heads the powerful General Office of the CCP Central Committee. This year, he also took charge of the Central Party School in Beijing. These positions place him almost constantly at Xi’s side.
Yet while some have seen Cai as more powerful than Li as a result, this is wrong. Frequent access to the supreme leader undoubtedly confers considerable influence over his schedule and the information reaching him. But proximity is not all in a system such as the CCP’s.
In Xi’s hierarchy of priorities, the party unquestionably takes precedence over the government. The party’s organizational apparatus, personnel system, disciplinary machinery, ideology, and security institutions directly determine whether Xi can sustain his hold on power. The economy may fluctuate, but political control over the party cannot be allowed to weaken. That is precisely why Xi entrusted the Secretariat and the General Office to Cai, whom he trusts deeply.
Yet this arrangement contains an easily overlooked paradox: It is precisely because party affairs are so important that Xi cannot fully delegate their core powers to Cai.
Cai coordinates, communicates, and supervises the implementation of central party affairs. But party affairs do not constitute a single domain that he can monopolize. Discipline inspection and anti-corruption work, personnel and organizational affairs, propaganda and ideology, political and legal affairs, and security are all overseen by other Xi loyalists, who report to the leader directly.
Moreover, last year Xi transferred Shi Taifeng, who had previously overseen united front work, to head the Central Committee Organization Department, which is responsible for evaluating and selecting party officials. Whether or not Xi intended the appointment to constrain Cai, it objectively limits Cai’s ability to turn the party apparatus into his own personal power base. The military, of course, remains under Xi’s direct control.
Nor does Cai’s responsibility for party affairs mean that Xi refrains from intervening directly. How far anti-corruption campaigns should go, what political standards officials must meet, and what ideological education campaigns the party should undertake are ultimately decided by Xi himself. Cai’s role is to translate Xi’s will into the party center’s daily operations.
Li, of course, operates under numerous constraints of his own. Xi has brought many major economic decisions under the direct authority of the party center through bodies such as the Central Financial and Economic Affairs Commission and the Central Financial Commission. Within the State Council, Vice Premiers Ding Xuexiang and He Lifeng, among others, oversee important portfolios and play major roles. These arrangements have dispersed some of the premier’s authority.
But the State Council differs fundamentally from the Secretariat and the General Office. It is a state institution with its own administrative system, legally defined powers, and vast implementing apparatus. The administration of the country—including economic, social, and cultural affairs, as well as foreign affairs and certain aspects of national defense—requires coordination and organization by the State Council.
Public administration, particularly economic management, involves an enormous number of concrete decisions. It requires reconciling conflicting interests among ministries and local governments and making choices as circumstances constantly change. Xi can determine broad policies and the overall direction of development, but he cannot personally run the government for Li every day. This gives Li a degree of discretion over day-to-day policy within the framework established by Xi.
With China confronting a lingering real estate crisis, local government debt, weak domestic demand, and sustained strategic pressure from the United States, Xi’s long-term ambitions cannot be realized without a functioning economy. An economic stagnation could also intensify social tensions and threaten stability. At certain stages, therefore, economic management may be no less important than political rectification. Party discipline and political loyalty can be reinforced through organizational measures, but economic growth cannot be restored by political declarations alone. Xi entrusted the State Council to Li, a longtime associate with extensive experience managing provincial economies because he needs someone who is both politically reliable and capable of getting things done.
Both men operate under Xi’s authority, but Li’s position as premier and the State Council’s distinct administrative machinery give him responsibilities for governing the country that Cai does not possess. Cai is unquestionably important to maintaining Xi’s personal grip on power, but he functions more as the chief manager of the party apparatus surrounding the supreme leader. His influence depends to a greater extent on Xi himself. Both lieutenants matter enormously, but proximity to Xi alone is no reason to reverse their relative positions.
Next year’s 21st Party Congress will provide a crucial test of whether this structure can endure. Both Li and Cai will have passed the customary retirement threshold of 68 by October 2027, but Li will be only three months beyond it, while Cai will be nearly four years over the limit. Under the long-standing informal retirement convention known as “seven up, eight down,” both would normally be expected to retire. Yet this convention is not an unbreakable rule.
Keeping both men on the Standing Committee, however, appears unlikely, since Xi must also make room for other loyalists to move up. My assessment is that Li has a stronger prospect of remaining on the Standing Committee—not simply because Cai is older but because the two men perform different political functions.
Cai, however, is unlikely to retire completely. He could follow the example of Chen Xi, who remained president of the Central Party School after leaving the Politburo. Cai might even simultaneously assume the largely ceremonial position of state vice president.
The question is whether Xi needs an aide who can help him govern the country or one who can help him control the party. As the challenges of governing the country grow more complex, his dependence on a lieutenant such as Li, who can actually manage those challenges, may only deepen. Next year’s party congress may be when this difference becomes clearest.

sources.headline: Xi’s Military Purges Make US Deterrence More Urgent
sources.text:
The Debate | Opinion | East Asia
“If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.”
China’s top military command has been almost emptied out. Of the seven members chosen for the Central Military Commission in 2022, only Xi Jinping and one general remain active. Days before Xi met U.S. President Donlald Trump in Washington last month, Beijing formally expelled Gen. Zhang Youxia, Xi’s longtime ally and former top military deputy, and Gen. Liu Zhenli, the former chief of the Joint Staff Department.
We do not know why Xi is doing this or what he intends to do next. But the purge has further strengthened his hand over the military. Reuters reported that analysts see Xi’s grip on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as strengthened by the removal of senior commanders and their protégés even as the upheaval weakens near-term readiness. If Xi chooses to invade Taiwan, impose a blockade, or undertake another act of military aggression in the region, more of that decision now rests with him. We do not know whether he will. That freer hand adds risk.
The scale of the purge is extraordinary. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that 41 of the 47 officers who held three-star rank in 2022 or were promoted afterward had been purged or potentially purged. Of the 35 three-star generals and admirals Xi promoted beginning in 2020, 32 had been investigated and 29 had been purged or potentially purged. Across the PLA, roughly 52 percent of senior leadership positions have been affected.
CSIS concluded that vacant posts and less experienced officers would complicate large-scale operations against Taiwan, including a blockade or amphibious assault. But we should not assume those complications will last. Taiwan’s defense ministry has warned of “rising unpredictability” in Chinese decision-making amid the purge. With this much upheaval in Beijing and more authority concentrated in Xi’s hands, steady, credible deterrence from Washington matters even more. Beijing should have no reason to believe an invasion, blockade or other act of aggression against Taiwan could succeed.
That means three things.
First, we should not answer upheaval in Beijing by creating upheaval at the Pentagon. One of America’s greatest military advantages is our professional officer corps, whose duty is to the constitution rather than a ruling party. Yet in 2025, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown along with five other senior generals and admirals. In April, Hegseth abruptly removed Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George with more than a year remaining in his term while American forces were fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon gave no public reason, and Reuters noted that removing a service chief during wartime is “extremely rare.” Experienced commanders who are prepared to give presidents unwelcome advice make our military stronger.
Second, our military resources have to match our priorities. The Iran war is draining weapons that matter for deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war had cost the Defense Department about $38 billion through August 1, with another month costing $2 billion to $3 billion depending on the intensity of fighting. More importantly, CBO found that heavy use of missile-defense interceptors will leave U.S. inventories reduced for several years and warned that the shortfall would be especially problematic in a conflict with China over Taiwan. If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.
Third, deterrence requires communication as well as strength. After air and maritime safety talks in May, U.S. and Chinese military representatives agreed that better communication could reduce miscalculations and the risk of unsafe encounters. With this much turnover at the top of the PLA, those channels matter even more.
We do not know Xi’s objectives. We know he has strengthened his own hand amid the uncertainty created by his purge of the military. Without any meaningful check on his power, Xi has a freer hand to pursue potentially more aggressive military decisions, adding risk to our relationship with the CCP.
Our job is not to guess Xi’s next move. It is to make sure Washington remains steady, with experienced military leadership, the weapons and forces needed to deter aggression, strong alliances, and reliable communication to keep a crisis from becoming a war.

sources.headline: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
sources.text:
On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.
The ad ran as a paid spot only once, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater. The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.
Formally titled ‘Peace, Little Girl,’ this political commercial was produced for President Lyndon B. Johnson’s 1964 campaign against Barry Goldwater.
I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Why campaigns use fear
Fear is an alarm. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.
When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.
Does fear change votes?
Sometimes, fear works.
During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.
Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.
More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.
Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.
The critical ingredient is empowerment
Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.
Gruesome warnings on tobacco products can spark fear – but what’s the next step?
Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images
For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.
My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.
Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.
One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.
The ‘Revolving Door’ ad attacked Democratic presidential candidate Michael Dukakis’ record on crime.
Bush’s campaign followed up with the “Revolving Door” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.
Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “The Race Card” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.
Gender works in a similar way.
In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security.
A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates.
Is fear a more common tactic now?
Using fear as a campaign tool is nothing new.
Anti-Andrew Jackson handbills circulated around the 1828 presidential election.
University of Pittsburgh/Wikimedia Commons
In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “Bear” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk.
What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.
The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.
Recent digital campaign data shows that negative ads are highly prized online because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily driven by user activity, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.
Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.

sources.headline: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
sources.text:
Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win.
President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “DOGE dividend” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues, and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans.
But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view.
For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races.
I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote.
Why vote buying rarely works
The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia.
By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants. Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s.
But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes.
If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence.
Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent.
As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “Against the Machine.”
The importance of competition
There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops.
First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights.
This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos.”
In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts.
AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell
The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets: Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision.
Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret.
It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment.
Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it.
Bringing it home
Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely.
Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate. There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism.
The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.”
At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vote to Republican.
In theory, there is one way Trump’s offer could succeed. Research shows that buying turnout, rather than trying to change vote choices, is routinely effective. But all the examples come from countries where party officials actively monitor who comes to the polls. Without that surveillance, which is illegal in the U.S., the free-rider problem could bedevil turnout as well.
But whether enacted or not, the promise of cash for votes has a big downside for democracy. It means that no one will know whether victorious Republican candidates won this November because Americans preferred their policies and gave them a mandate – or because they expected to get paid.

sources.headline: Why the ‘Odds of Mischief Are High’ in These Midterms
sources.text:
With U.S. President Donald Trump’s approval rating at record lows amid high inflation spiked by an unpopular war, many pundits view the upcoming midterm elections as the only serious emergency brake left for the nation.
But even if, as expected, Democrats win substantial victories in the House and possibly the Senate—and if Trump doesn’t follow through on his threats to call it fraud and somehow nullify the vote—the nation may still be heading into a political morass.
Rather than rallying around a common direction—other than opposition to Trump—the Democratic Party appears to lack anything like a coherent governing philosophy or compelling leadership. On the contrary, even on the verge of victory on Nov. 3, Democrats seem to be coming apart at the seams ideologically, making a party that is fractious in the best of times much more so today. It is racked by deep fissures between moderates and candidates allied with left-wing populist forces such as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), including major divisions over taxes, health care, and Israel.
In a bruising Senate primary race in Michigan, for example, most establishment Democrats backed Rep. Haley Stevens, a moderate. The DSA-aligned candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, a public health official who ran on a progressive platform of Medicare for All and major new taxes on the rich, barely squeaked out a win. That costly battle, along with El-Sayed’s controversial criticism of Israel, has dampened his support among centrist voters in a tightening race against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers. The state’s former Democratic chair, Lon Johnson, even urged Michiganders not to vote for El-Sayed, saying that doing so would surrender “our party to ideological extremism.”
A person stands in front of a large American flag spread out as a backdrop, gesturing with their arms outstretched.
Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed holds a campaign town hall event in Ionia, Michigan, on Oct. 11.Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images
“The Democrats have this incredible capacity to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory,” said Sidney Milkis, a political scientist at the University of Virginia. “I’m worried about voters’ reaction to the Democratic socialist insurgency. Michigan’s a really important race for control of the Senate. El-Sayed is a good candidate, but he has a lot of baggage.”
Many younger voters are openly dismissive of those who, in the absence of any other national figure, remain placeholders at the top of the party: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. (Schumer’s unfavorability ratings have soared since 2025, and Jeffries’s ratings are only slightly better.)
Much of the party’s direction depends on the size of the Democratic victory, if one occurs, especially in the House. “If it’s narrow, then Jeffries is going to be under pressure from those very far left folks, the DSA, but if it’s large, he can tell them to pound sand,” said Matt Bennett of the Third Way, a centrist Democratic think tank. “But either way, the identity of a party is forged by presidential politics not congressional. What will determine what Democrats are is the presidential primary process.”
That quadrennial beauty contest will get underway early next year. But it is difficult to identify a party savior with a centrist, electable national platform on the order of U.S. Presidents Barack Obama or Bill Clinton—or even Joe Biden.
Much of the charisma and star power grabbing headlines today comes from the far left—with new faces like New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and others affiliated with the DSA—despite the broad mass of Democrats remaining closer to the center.
That could leave the party vulnerable to a 2028 GOP strategy of tarring Democrats as “communists” or too leftist to govern, possibly costing the election for whoever becomes the party standard-bearer. In the last week, Trump and other Republicans lost no time in painting the violent protests in France as a warning of what could happen in the United States at the hands of left-wing ideologues supporting open immigration and infected by Islamist radicalism.
“When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America,” Trump said in Kansas on Oct. 19. (The French government said the demonstrations have more to do with high prices, especially soaring energy costs, driven up by Trump’s war in Iran.)
Still, most political experts would say there’s a long way to go to 2028. “If you’d asked me after the midterms in 1990, I wouldn’t have known Bill Clinton was coming along to save our party,” Bennett said. “Someone is going to emerge.”
Ossoff, a man in jeans and a blue shirt, stands on a stage holding a hand to his chest, with a microphone, podium, and American flags visible in the background.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff walks onstage to speak during a midterm election rally in Atlanta, Georgia, United States, on Oct. 17. Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images
Leading moderate Democratic candidates are clearly vying for a national platform. Among them is Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who has made his Senate race a blunt test of whether the country is willing to endure a “crook president and his crook family,” as Ossoff said at a rally on Oct. 19. “They promised to drain the swamp. Instead, it’s the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it.”
The fierce divisions within the Democratic Party suggest that even a victorious slate on Nov. 3 would likely end up, once again, defaulting to a least common denominator policy of attacking and investigating Trump.
“The problem is that the party overall enjoys such low levels of approval and trust, even among partisan Democrats themselves, and is characterized by a such a collective quality of leaderless and directionless rule … that the party has little capacity to handle internal disagreements,” said Sam Rosenfeld, a professor at Colgate University and co-author of The Hollow Parties: The Many Pasts and Disordered Present of American Party Politics.
“Democrats have spent a decade reacting to Republican provocations instead of building something worth believing in,” Sarah Longwell, a prominent anti-Trump Republican, wrote in her new book, How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time. “Ask swing voters what they want from the Democratic Party, and you’ll hear a version of this over and over: Tell us what you’re for.”
Hence next month’s midterm election is largely a battle of negative perceptions that will almost certainly be decided by which party’s reputation is less bad.
“It’s definitely true that the Democrats’ commanding position in the midterms does not reflect much in the way of underlying political strength and popularity,” Rosenfeld said.
There have been attempts to bridge the ideological gaps within the party, but none have taken hold. Few any longer tout an “abundance” agenda popularized last year by the pundit Ezra Klein or so-called supply-side progressivism. The movement to eliminate red tape preventing new infrastructure and construction has lost momentum in the face of public resistance to building data centers.
Another big question is whether Democrats will control the Senate, which remains a close-run affair. “That, to me, is really crucial,” Milkis said. “The Senate has a lot more control over the judiciary and appointments. That would make it much more difficult for Trump to appoint a new [U.S. Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth.”
So, how will it all play out on Nov. 3?
Trump, wearing a red cap with white letters that say USA, speaks at a podium with a microphone, with a reflection of an American flag, slightly blurred, overlaying the scene.
Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, on Oct. 16. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
Many experts see the midterm elections as yet another “fulcrum point” for U.S. democracy. That resurrects an overused phrase popularized by Biden during the Trump era.
“This election offers a choice to voters about whether they want constitutional government or not,” said Justin Levitt, an election expert at Loyola Marymount University and former senior policy advisor for democracy and voting rights in the Biden administration.
In recent weeks, Trump’s poll numbers have been trending steadily down. A poll published on Oct. 21 by the New York Times and Siena University showed that 36 percent of likely voters approved of his performance, a new bottom for that survey, while the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Oct. 19 found that Trump’s approval rating has plunged to a record low of 31 percent.
Those numbers have led some Republicans to fear a blowout like the 2006 midterms that gave Democrats both the House and Senate on the back of U.S. President George W. Bush’s deep unpopularity. As Trump has done in Iran, Bush was mired in a highly criticized and costly war of choice in Iraq, and he was dogged by various Republican political scandals and legislative defeats.
This time, a net gain of just four seats in both the House and Senate would do the trick of shifting power, erasing Republicans’ ​218-214 and 53-47 majorities.
Another key question is whether Trump’s plunging numbers—if they precipitate a GOP defeat like what Bush called his “thumping” in 2006—will begin to loosen his decade-long stranglehold on the Republican Party. The president himself has set the stage for his own comeuppance by telling voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and relentlessly campaigning across the country. But several establishment Republicans have split from him on Iran and his trade war with Canada. They have also criticized his recent moves to accommodate Russian President Vladimir Putin by waiving sanctions on diesel imports and withdrawing support for Ukraine.
Then there’s the question of whether Trump will even accept the results. “If there’s free and fair election and kind of a transfer of power, it can send a signal to Americans and people around the world that the United States is not destined for a Jan. 6 at every contested election,” said Matthew Dallek, a political scientist at George Washington University, referring to Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election results by calling on his supporters to prevent the certification of Biden’s win (which he failed to do).
“At the same time, there is no single election that can repair the damage to America’s image in the world as a defender of democracy and reliable ally or repair the lost faith of Americans in the ability of government to improve their lives,” Dallek said.
Milkis added: “Right now, I think the country is in the most danger it’s been in since the Civil War, really, given the current polarization.”
Experts are projecting several possible outcomes along a spectrum marked by cautious hopefulness at one end and utter disaster at the other.
The hopeful scenario—call it “back from the brink”—would usher in huge Democratic victories, render Trump a badly weakened and lame-duck president, and perhaps offer a glimmer of a way out of Trumpism and back to constitutionalism.
The other end of the spectrum—call it “into the abyss”—could mean that Trump manages to follow through with plans to conduct massive vote manipulation and fraud, denial of election results, possibly even an attempt to declare a national emergency and send in troops under the Insurrection Act, which permits the use of regular military domestically.
“It seems evident that there are no guardrails erected around him at all,” Bennett said. “The craziest of the crazies are talking to him. Anything is possible, and Trump has proven that, in this term, he’s willing to do basically anything. I think the odds of mischief are high.”

sources.headline: Could AI Disinformation Disrupt the Midterms?
sources.text:
Elections in the United States have been a battleground for foreign adversaries dating back at least a decade, with Russia, Iran, and China all using cyberattacks and social media campaigns to disrupt or interfere with the voting process. Add in the advanced cyber capabilities of the latest artificial intelligence models, their ability to generate bespoke information on command, and a highly polarized electorate, and the upcoming U.S. midterm elections begin to look like a potential minefield of misinformation.
But the overarching message from more than half a dozen experts whom Foreign Policy spoke to, including current and former tech executives and government officials, is that it’s not time to press the panic button just yet.
Elections in the United States have been a battleground for foreign adversaries dating back at least a decade, with Russia, Iran, and China all using cyberattacks and social media campaigns to disrupt or interfere with the voting process. Add in the advanced cyber capabilities of the latest artificial intelligence models, their ability to generate bespoke information on command, and a highly polarized electorate, and the upcoming U.S. midterm elections begin to look like a potential minefield of misinformation.
But the overarching message from more than half a dozen experts whom Foreign Policy spoke to, including current and former tech executives and government officials, is that it’s not time to press the panic button just yet.
“There are attempts to use AI to deceive, certainly, but they haven’t been particularly effective,” said Matt Masterson, a senior director for elections and societal resilience at Microsoft. “I haven’t seen anything that’s really taken hold in this election cycle or jumped out at me as really having an impact in that way.”
That’s not to say that U.S. adversaries couldn’t be—or aren’t already—using AI tools to make their disinformation campaigns more effective. Large language models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini (to name only a few) give bad actors the ability to operate at a speed and scale that they previously couldn’t.
“It’s helped them operationalize their work and almost industrialize it—it means that they can spin up content more quickly. They can also do a lot of research more effectively and quickly in terms of their target audience,” said Olga Belogolova, the director of the emerging technologies initiative at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies.
Investigators have uncovered past Russian and Iranian campaigns because of mistranslations into English or a lack of knowledge of local slang. But AI allows those actors to sound more authentic on social media.
“A lot of what we’re seeing on the back end is changing because it’s helping them draft and polish content, translate, and localize things, which are important changes. I’m not trying to dismiss them,” Belogolova said. “But that doesn’t mean that they’re necessarily going to be any better at persuading and reaching people,” she added. That’s in part because the social and even traditional media channels that they rely on to distribute the content remain the same. “A lot of what you see on the receiving end of information consumption hasn’t changed dramatically.”
Midterm elections in the United States also pose a fundamentally different challenge from an interference standpoint than U.S. presidential elections, such as the one in 2024.
“Midterms are not as easy to target or as popular to target by foreign adversaries. Our federal system, with 400-plus congressional races and 30-something Senate races, makes it hard to target effectively,” said Jacob Breach, a senior advisor at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies think tank who previously spent 15 years in the U.S. intelligence community focused largely on foreign influence operations. “They’re testing grounds for actors’ unique tactics and unique combinations of tactics to attempt to interfere or influence these elections, but it’s not like it would be in a presidential election year.”
Iran and Russia are also engaged in protracted wars that could reduce their wherewithal to target the midterms. AI can help ease that load, but only so much.
“These actors have limited capabilities and bandwidth. When those actors are distracted by other things, like the wars in this case, they have less bandwidth to devote to sustained campaigns,” Breach said.
A voting station featuring several voting booths draped with red, white, and blue striped curtains. On the right, a person in an orange shirt and athletic shorts leans over a table using a white voting privacy shield emblazoned with an American flag and the word "VOTE."
Voters cast their ballots in the primary for midterm elections in Sanbornton, New Hampshire, United States, on Sept. 8. CJ Gunther/Getty Images
Multiple experts told Foreign Policy that companies, election officials, and voters are simply better prepared this time around to combat misinformation—including by using AI as a solution on the defensive side.
“Back in 2024, it was a rare election official who was really thinking about AI for good—I think most of us were laser focused on deepfakes and the concerns associated with that,” said Bill Gates, who served as a supervisor for Arizona’s Maricopa County during five successive elections until 2024 and is no stranger to election integrity efforts.
Gates (no relation to the billionaire Microsoft founder) now heads Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Lab, which has launched an initiative sponsored by Microsoft to train election officials in AI applications and harness AI to provide voters with authoritative information.
“The sort of burying-the-head-in-the-sand ostrich approach that maybe a fair number of us were doing in 2024, you’re seeing a lot less of that this time around,” Gates said.
The ASU partnership is one of several that major tech companies have entered into to ensure that their models can serve reliable information. OpenAI has partnered with The Associated Press to supply its vote count data to ChatGPT users who ask about it, while OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft have all partnered with an organization called Democracy Works, which aims to provide tech companies with reliable information about polling place locations and other frequent queries by prospective voters.
OpenAI and Anthropic say they have also tested their models extensively to prevent political bias and clamp down on bad actors’ potential misuse of their platforms. “People should be able to access reliable information, understand the origin of AI-generated media that they might encounter off platform, and … explore political questions without being steered in one particular direction by the model,” Josh Lawson, OpenAI’s head of civic and strategic risk, told reporters in a recent briefing. Combating adversaries requires “adding friction in strategic areas” that make it harder for them to exploit the chatbots. “Bad actors have a lot of options whenever they choose to fly. We don’t want them to fly with us.”
In an encouraging sign, a study published by the Brennan Center for Justice found in August that most of the popular chatbots consistently pushed back against common election conspiracy theories.
The pace at which AI is evolving and the so-called “black box” nature of the technology mean that unforeseen consequences and threats are always a possibility.
“The hardest thing is that we don’t know what we don’t know,” said Katie Harbath, author of the new book Disrupting Politics: A Front Row Seat to the Collision of Technology and Democracy, which is about her decade leading Facebook’s election-focused public policy team until 2021. “You can do as much as possible to try to be ready for any of these potential things, but what if something happens that we weren’t prepared for?” she asked. “The thing that I’m most happy about—I don’t know if that’s the right word—is the fact that there are a lot of people thinking about this.”
A hand holds a smartphone displaying a social media video in front of computer screens showing political media feeds and images. On the smartphone is an AI-generated video showing a remarkably in-shape President Trump kicking a man while fighting him.
A composite photo illustration shows an array of AI-generated images posted on pro-Trump AI influencers’ social media accounts in 2026. Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images
That also extends to the platform users and voters themselves, for whom AI-generated content has become a part of life. That has led to a natural skepticism that many experts say is somewhat healthy—provided that it doesn’t tip over into distrusting even authoritative information.
“I do think that the prevalence of AI-manufactured and -created information is causing people to at least look twice at what they’re seeing,” Breach said.
“Societally, it’s not great. I would love to be able to trust what I saw on the internet,” he added. But “if AI is causing Americans to get better at media literacy simply because they trust what they’re seeing less, that’s a good thing.”

sources.headline: For weeks, deepfake celebrities have been telling Americans not to vote for Democrats in the midterm elections. U.S. intelligence says Russia is behind it.
sources.text: Russia has mounted an online campaign to discredit candidates for the U.S. Congress ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes told Politico. Both are Democrats who sit on their chambers’ intelligence committees.The lawmakers said their conclusions about Russian interference come from a classified U.S. intelligence report they received earlier in the week. The report says Moscow is using AI tools to spread disinformation and undermine trust in individual candidates and in the elections as a whole.The lawmakers believe Russia could target both Democrats and Republicans who support Ukraine. The intelligence agencies have found no proven attempts by Russia to hack the election system or campaign networks.Reports of attempts to interfere in the congressional elections first surfaced in early September. The Bot Blocker project, which tracks pro-Russian bot activity on social media, warned about AI-generated videos featuring deepfakes of celebrities such as Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts, and Cher urging viewers not to vote for Democrats.According to the project, a Russian bot network called “Matryoshka” is spreading the videos. The clips were posted on X under the logos of real news outlets and contained false accusations against American politicians.Posts from Russian bots on X rack up tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of views, but those figures are artificially inflated through fake engagement, Bloomberg reported. The clips can reach up to 200,000 views in the first hour, after which the view counts stop moving entirely. Moreover, the posts draw almost no likes or reposts.Researchers from Graphika, Alethea, and Clemson University identified another Russian bot network spreading deepfake videos that targeted American politicians, NBC News reported. On October 20, videos appeared on X baselessly accusing Texas Democrat James Talarico of sexual assault, and one post garnered more than 1.3 million views.The researchers said the network behind it is a Russian disinformation operation called “Storm-1516” that has been linked to Russian military intelligence. “Storm-1516” has previously been accused of interfering in elections in the United States, Germany, Hungary, and France.At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

sources.headline: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
sources.text: Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections."This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America". The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members while speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House."After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough'," the former president said in Cleveland. Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy. "If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs" and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

sources.headline: Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
sources.text: The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan."I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive.Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan". The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year. In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator. "Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign. He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot. Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit. The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections. The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

sources.headline: US Attorney General Todd Blanche defends Alaska Senate election lawsuit
sources.text: United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race.On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump’s approval ratings plummet: what that means for the US midtermslist 2 of 3Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaskalist 3 of 3Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?end of listIn each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration.“ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters.“We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.”But the Justice Department’s lawsuit, filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism.Many have accused the administration of President Donald Trump of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit.“I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday.Inside the Alaska Senate raceDuring the midterm elections on November 3, citizens in Alaska will vote in one of the closest Senate races in the country, which will help decide whether Republicans maintain their majority in the chamber.Senator Dan S Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is seeking to defend his seat in the US Senate. But he faces fierce competition from former US Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat.Also in the running is another candidate named Dan J Sullivan, a former Forest Service employee.The second Sullivan’s decision to run has raised concerns that he is a spoiler candidate, whose presence on the ballot is designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.But the Forest Service worker has denied any such intent. Such allegations, he said, are “entirely false”.“I am not a registered Democrat, and I have had no conversations whatsoever with the Peltola campaign about my candidacy,” the second Sullivan wrote in a letter to Alaska’s lieutenant governor before the state’s primaries.“I have considered running for political office for over a decade. I made the decision to formally run for the United States Senate in the upcoming primary election because Senator Sullivan has routinely failed the people of Alaska, and they deserve a better representative. It is my right to do so.”Four candidates advanced to the final round of voting after Alaska’s August primaries. They included Peltola and both Sullivans. The two men are running as Republicans.A controversial lawsuitThe Justice Department has argued that its lawsuit – filed less than two weeks before the midterm elections – is necessary “to protect the integrity” of the election.Any result in the Senate race, it argues, would be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan”.The department has therefore called on the US District Court in Alaska to issue an order declaring the race’s certification “unlawful” and barring the state from “allowing such a certification to occur”.Under the US Constitution, only states have the power to administer elections, though Congress has the right to pass regulations concerning federal votes.It is highly unusual for a presidential administration to inject itself into issues of state election certification, and experts say such a move is likely to be deemed illegal.Already, in June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could compete in the Senate race. The state’s Division of Elections has also taken steps to reduce voter confusion.The November 3 ballot, for instance, will list Dan S Sullivan as the incumbent and as a “registered Republican”.Dan J Sullivan, meanwhile, will have the suffix “Jr” added to his name, and his party affiliation will be left blank, despite the candidate identifying as Republican.But in Sunday’s television appearances, Blanche — who leads the Department of Justice and formerly served as Trump’s personal lawyer — argued that merely having two Sullivans on the ballot is a recipe for confusion.“It is wrong,” Blanche told CNN. “Putting aside whether we’re going to win or lose in the courts, putting aside what the Alaskan Supreme Court has done, in our system, we should not have a candidate who has to worry about another candidate being on the ballot for no other reason than to confuse voters.”Blanche also denied any impropriety in Trump saying he ordered the lawsuit.“He’s supposed to make sure that everything in this country is running right, including elections,” Blanche said.The race for the SenateHistorically, the Justice Department has embraced a norm of judicial independence, though critics have accused the Trump administration of wielding its prosecutorial powers for political gain.Bash, the CNN host, raised some of those concerns, pointing to Trump’s comments accusing Democrats of cheating, as well as his history of election denialism.The president has long denied his loss in the 2020 presidential race, and his supporters sought to block the certification of that election, notably by storming the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.When Bash pointed to that incident, Blanche chided her: “Oh, you’ve got to stop it with that.”“Why are you yelling at me?” Bash responded as the two talked over each other.“You are not being a real person. Come on, man,” Blanche continued. “That is crazy.”He also denied that Trump was setting the stage for a contested election if the Democrat Peltola were to win. Instead, he framed the lawsuit as setting the stage for further investigations into any eventual results.“The relief that we’re seeking – which, again, isn’t to determine who the senator is, it’s not to try to overturn something the state is going to do – it’s just to make sure that the ballots that come in are kept in a way that may allow a court to investigate further,” Blanche said.Speaking to CBS, Blanche also dodged a question about whether Trump personally asked him to file the lawsuit.“I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States. I never have, and I never will,” Blanche said.The race to control the US Senate is expected to be a nail-biter, with Republicans holding a slim majority at present: They have 53 seats in the 100-member chamber.Only a third of the Senate’s seats – 35 in total – will be up for grabs in the midterm races, as terms in the chamber last six years and are staggered across different election years.Trump’s Republican Party is projected to face an uphill battle to protect its congressional majorities, amid backlash against the rising cost of living and Trump’s own withering poll numbers.Roughly seven Senate elections are considered toss-ups, including the Alaska race.In early October, The New York Times and Siena College released a poll finding Peltola leading the incumbent Sullivan by nearly 7 percentage points, one of the widest margins of any of the toss-up states.
