sources.headline: Palestinian citizens face a painful choice in Israel’s election: To vote or not
sources.text:
Elections are typically framed as a choice for voters. For Palestinian citizens of Israel, however, the country’s national ballots pose more of a dilemma.
Constituting about one-sixth of eligible voters in Israel, Palestinian citizens could hold the difference in a race expected to be close. But voting involves a trade-off: By casting a ballot for their best interests, many Palestinian citizens believe they also risk legitimizing a process that seeks to silence their voice and a system that treats their citizenship as conditional.
The coming Israeli election on Oct. 27, 2026, brings that tension to a new peak. Since the last general election in 2022, the destruction and mass killing in Gaza, restrictions on Palestinian citizens’ speech and protest and leading opposition parties’ rejection of having Arab political partners have sharpened the dilemma of seeking protection through institutions that reinforce their exclusion.
Having devoted most of my academic career to studying relations between Israel and its Palestinian citizens, I see the question facing Palestinian citizens of Israel as part of a much longer struggle over survival, citizenship and political belonging.
Citizenship as protection
The approximate 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel – out of a total population of around 10 million Israeli citizens and 15 million people living under Israeli direct or indirect control – are largely the descendants of Arabs who stayed on land that became the state of Israel.
The category excludes the descendants of 750,000 Palestinians who were forced from their homes during the Arab-Israeli war of 1948 – most of whom were prevented from returning.
A hurried wartime census dated Nov. 8, 1948, helped determine who would be recognized as belonging to the new state. Registration and subsequent citizenship requirements excluded anyone who was absent from their home at the time of the census. This included Palestinians who had sought temporary shelter in neighboring countries or elsewhere in what was Mandatory Palestine.
Therefore, the census did more than count residents: In most cases, Palestinians displaced by the war who were absent when it was conducted were excluded from the population register. That made it almost impossible for them to obtain citizenship and return to their homes.
For those who remained, citizenship became a form of insurance against expulsion; once they were designated as citizens of Israel, their removal became legally much more difficult.
Despite its shortcomings – and its failure to prevent dispossession and repression – Israeli citizenship has still been taken particularly seriously by Palestinian citizens.
A Palestinian citizen of Israel casts a votes in the 2022 Israeli legislative election.
Photo by Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images
Fluctuations in political influence
Palestinians today constitute approximately half the population in the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea: Israel, Gaza and the Occupied West Bank. But fewer than one-third of them possess Israeli citizenship. Those who do – and as such can participate in its national elections – constitute roughly 17% of Israel’s citizenry.
From the creation of the Israeli state onward, Palestinian citizens have been eligible to vote, but they have faced hurdles to full participation.
Since the 1970s, Palestinian politicians’ identification with the wider Palestinian struggle has prompted attempts to disqualify candidates and parties. The Supreme Court has generally blocked such exclusions.
In Israel’s first decades, most Palestinian votes went to the Jewish-Arab Communist Party, in its various incarnations, or to Arab lists – parties affiliated with the ruling Labor movement and acting on its behalf. The 1980s saw the disappearance of these satellite lists and the emergence of alternatives to the communists. For example, the Progressive List for Peace entered parliament in 1984, combining Palestinian nationalism with Jewish-Arab cooperation. Later, in 1988, the Arab Democratic Party emerged as an exclusively Arab party.
Except for short periods in the mid-1990s and 2021-2022, Israeli parties that consider themselves Zionist generally regarded none of these independent lists as legitimate coalition partners. But Palestinian parliamentary leverage reached a high point in 1992–1995, when Yitzhak Rabin’s government relied on support from two Arab-majority parties.
They pursued two connected goals: advancing what became known as the Oslo peace process in the hope that it would lead to Palestinian statehood, and reducing discrimination in funding communities.
Their leverage helped secure significant increases in public investment for Arab communites. Similarly, the short-lived anti-Netanyahu government of 2021–2022 relied on the support of an Arab party, enabling some limited improvements on local issues.
A narrowing political arena
Today, space for such Palestinian parliamentary influence appears narrower than it has been for decades, Since the early 2010s, moreover, Arab parties have increasingly faced official and unofficial attempts to neuter their influence.
In September, Israel’s Central Elections Committee sought to disqualify both Arab electoral lists – the Joint List and the United Arab List – as well as individual candidates. In the 2022 election, these lists’ constituent parties received approximately 86% of the votes cast in Arab localities. Disqualifying both lists would have deprived the vast majority of Palestinian voters of their preferred political representation.
The Supreme Court reversed the lists’ disqualifications but signaled that a majority of its judges would uphold the exclusion of the National Democratic Assembly’s leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, over an article he wrote immediately after the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023. His critics interpreted it as endorsing the massacre of Israeli civilians, though Abu Shehadeh and others vigorously denied that claim.
Rather than demand a ruling, Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy, explaining that he feared a damaging precedent that would restrict Palestinian political activity more broadly.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, leader of the Balad party.
Erik Marmor/Getty Images
This exclusionary atmosphere extends beyond political institutions. In the Israel Democracy Institute’s July 2026 survey, about one-third of Jewish respondents opposed Arab citizens’ right to vote. Among supporters of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition parties, the proportion was approximately 55%.
Palestinian voters have also faced intimidation and voter suppression. Practical barriers compound this pressure. Residents of unrecognized Bedouin villages, for example, face long journeys to assigned polling stations.
The costs of participation – and abstention
While many Palestinians understand that participation legitimizes electoral rules under which their choices are limited, abstention surrenders opportunities to address issues such as the rise of organized crime and violent crime in Arab communities.
And although Palestinian parties could hold the balance of who gets to form a coalition, the reality is not that simple.
The differences between Netanyahu and much of his opposition regarding Palestinians’ rights and self-determination are largely that of style rather than policy. Neither Netanyahu’s ruling coalition nor the leading opposition parties support a two-state solution or offer any other credible route to ending the occupation.
Nevertheless, the main opposition depends more heavily on a secular middle class sensitive to global opinion that is increasingly turning against Israel over the dispossession and killing of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
This may be an exceptionally low threshold of expectation, but it reflects the choices available for Palestinian voters on such issues related to Palestinians living under occupation.
Personal security at home is an even more pressing concern for many Palestinian citizens of Israel. Criminal organizations terrorize Arab communities, while killings have reached unprecedented levels under the current government – largely through state complicity.
In a May survey, more than half of Arab respondents identified violence in their communities as the principal factor negatively affecting their mood. The urgency of this crisis helps explain widespread support for Arab participation in the next government – some 77% of the Arab citizens support this arrangement, which most Zionist opposition parties reject.
Can turnout shift the balance?
For Palestinian citizens, the electoral options remain limited. The United Arab List, a party rooted in the Muslim Brotherhood, now most explicitly advocates integration into Israel’s governing institutions. Seeking acceptance by Jewish parties, it has largely set aside Palestinian national rhetoric to prioritize its constituents’ immediate needs.
The Joint List, meanwhile, brings together nationalist and communist forces seeking to make Israeli citizenship substantive through equal rights, without abandoning explicit manifestations of Palestinian national identity and solidarity with other Palestinians. Its constituent parties disagree over how far cooperation with Zionist parties should extend.
Voting for a Zionist party remains another option, but its appeal has diminished sharply over recent decades. Such a trend, however diminished, persists particularly among constituencies with close institutional ties to the state.
Finally, Arab voters can abstain, and roughly 35% to 45% are expected to do so, compared with 25% to 30% among Jewish voters.
Palestinian voters abstain for reasons ranging from apathy to a deliberate boycott of the state established through their people’s dispossession. Recent attempts to suppress Arab representation could either mobilize citizens who feel their remaining protections slipping away or deepen their reluctance to participate in an arena so visibly stacked against them.
The outcome could shape the election, and Arab party leaders aspire to 70% turnout. Higher participation would increase Arab representation and could push marginal right-wing parties below the electoral threshold, weakening Netanyahu’s prospects of forming a government.
The hope of Arab party leaders is that, despite opposition leaders’ declarations against cooperation, a sufficiently large Arab parliamentary bloc will leave the Jewish opposition parties little choice but to seek its support to remove Netanyahu.

sources.headline: Netanyahu Vows to Overthrow Iranian Regime
sources.text:
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Israel preparing for new strikes on Iran, anti-government protests in Serbia, and political violence in Australia.
Netanyahu Echoes Call for Regime Change in Iran
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave a forceful directive to the country’s military and security agencies just days before a critical parliamentary election. His message: overthrow the Iranian regime.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Israel preparing for new strikes on Iran, anti-government protests in Serbia, and political violence in Australia.
Netanyahu Echoes Call for Regime Change in Iran
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu gave a forceful directive to the country’s military and security agencies just days before a critical parliamentary election. His message: overthrow the Iranian regime.
“There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all,” Netanyahu told new officers of the Israel Defense Forces at their graduation ceremony on Wednesday, arguing that as long as Iran’s current leadership remains, Israel faces an “existential threat.”
That objective is nothing new. For years, Netanyahu has described Iran’s existence as a threat to Israel’s security, citing its common refrain of “death to Israel” and arguing that Tehran seeks to develop a nuclear weapons program. Iran’s repeated insistence that its nuclear advancements are only for civilian purposes has done little to assuage Israel’s fears.
Now, with Netanyahu’s Likud party facing a crucial parliamentary vote on Oct. 27, the right-wing leader is turning to a tried-and-true playbook to try and secure enough votes to remain in power.
The election will be the first one since Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. The attack ultimately led to devastating conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran—all of which have sparked fierce condemnation from rights activists who have accused Israeli forces of perpetrating war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
Many analysts see the vote as a litmus test on Netanyahu’s leadership, including his handling of the deadliest attack on Israeli soil since its founding and his headstrong approach to some of the world’s biggest institutions, such as the United Nations. By focusing on Iran’s continued threat to Israel, Netanyahu hopes that he can convince voters why his Likud party should be in office.
Israeli forces have stepped up training exercises with the United States to double down on this messaging. On Monday, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise visit to Ovda Air Base in southern Israel, meeting with Netanyahu. On Wednesday, U.S. officials told the New York Times that joint strikes against Iran are expected to resume after the U.S. midterm elections next month.
Iran “is truly an Evil Regime, and I can only hope the American Public, and the World, understands how EVIL they are!” U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday, echoing Netanyahu’s command that Tehran must never have a nuclear weapon.
In response, the Iranian regime denounced a return to active fighting. “We see the next conflict as an existential threat,” said Mehdi Mohammadi, an advisor to top Iranian negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. “The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines.’”
Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s security council, added that fresh U.S.-Israeli attacks will result in Iranian strikes on oil facilities, undersea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across as many as seven Persian Gulf countries.
Today’s Most Read
The Iran War Has Changed the World Forever by Kenneth M. Pollack
Myths of Battlefield Triumph Are Destroying the U.S. Military by Gil Barndollar and Jason Dempsey
How Ukraine Is Navigating Trump’s Latest U-Turn by Keith Johnson
What We’re Following
Vucic’s biggest challenge yet? Thousands of Serbian students held their final campaign rally in the capital of Belgrade on Thursday ahead of snap parliamentary elections on Sunday. The youth-led movement aims to challenge authoritarian leader Aleksandar Vucic, who resigned from the presidency last month so that he could pursue the prime minister’s office.
Anti-government protests first erupted in November 2024, when a collapsed railway station canopy killed 16 people. Demonstrators accused Belgrade of poor state oversight, negligence, and corruption. In response, Vucic launched a fierce crackdown on political dissent, using excessive force, arbitrary arrests, and digital repression to undermine the protests.
Still, the youth-led movement never fully disappeared. Polling suggests a tight race between Vucic’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and the Student List group, even with Vucic earning the support of the United States.
Sunday’s vote could be the biggest political threat to Vucic’s reign since he came to power in 2014. He served as prime minister for three years before becoming president in 2017. During that time, democratic freedoms in Serbia have steadily dropped, with Freedom House, the World Press Freedom Index, and Transparency International all noting record declines.
Political violence in Australia. On Thursday, Australian authorities charged a man with threatening a lawmaker’s staff with a weapon, just days after another parliamentarian was targeted in a historically rare political attack. Threats against Australian politicians and their offices doubled between 2021 and 2025.
Australian lawmakers are among the most publicly accessible in the world, but the recent spate of attacks has convinced some experts that this tradition may need to be reconsidered, especially for women politicians.
Earlier this week, lawmaker Helen Haines was hit by a Toyota Land Cruiser outside of her office in the state of Victoria, leaving her in critical condition. Both her legs were amputated. Then, on Thursday, a 56-year-old man entered the office of Hannah Beazley, a Western Australian representative, and demanded to speak to her while wielding wooden sticks. No one was injured.
The two attacks do not appear connected, but they prompted Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to denounce rising political violence during a recent briefing on misogynistic threats targeting lawmakers. “There has been a normalization of behavior that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn’t happening a couple of decades ago,” Albanese said.
State Department evacuation orders. The U.S. State Department ordered nonessential embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as Houthi strikes risk escalating regional tensions. Several U.S. embassies in other Gulf countries are already under “restricted operations” that limit the number of personnel stationed there.
“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against ​Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott wrote on X on Wednesday.
That includes recent deadly assaults on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and heavy strikes on Saudi energy facilities. The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh was already working with a skeleton crew after a drone strike in March badly damaged the building, and Washington had ordered its diplomats to refrain from using any Saudi airport without special permission.
Still, U.S. personnel had begun returning to their posts in recent months as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi rebels reignited.
Odds and Ends
For more than a month, South Korean authorities have tried to free a female dusky shark trapped in a canal in the port city of Busan. From spraying water to deploying nets, officials have resorted to several unsuccessful tactics to encourage Bukangi, named after the city’s North Port, to swim back out to sea.
On Wednesday, a floating platform finally managed to herd Bukangi out of the canal. However, celebrations did not last long, as the huge shark swam right back into the port overnight on Thursday. Experts argue that it is critical for the animal to return to open water, but it appears that Bukangi isn’t finished visiting the city.

sources.headline: Russian anti-war rock musician Andrey Makarevich endorses Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of election, drawing backlash
sources.text: Israel will hold parliamentary elections on October 27. Recent opinion polls show Likud, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, trailing Yashar, the party led by former Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot. Neither party has a decisive lead, however.A few days before the election, Netanyahu posted a recording of a conversation with musician Andrey Makarevich, who has lived in Israel for the past several years. Makarevich, who holds both Israeli and Russian citizenship, expressed support for Netanyahu during the conversation.Many people in Israel and beyond were unhappy with Makarevich’s support for Netanyahu, who divides opinion among Israelis. Some Israelis are dissatisfied with the prime minister’s domestic policies, as well as his government’s actions before, during, and after the Hamas terrorist attack on October 7, 2023.“Wow, what a storm this has stirred up! A typhoon! A tsunami!” Makarevich wrote on social media.Critics noted that the musician had supported Vladimir Putin in the early 2000s and that in 2008, his band, Mashina Vremeni, had taken part in the “Forward, Russia!” rally and concert on Moscow’s Vasilyevsky Spusk to celebrate Dmitry Medvedev’s presidential election victory. Makarevich later publicly criticized the Russian authorities on many occasions. In 2022, the musician, who spoke out against the war with Ukraine, was designated a “foreign agent” in Russia.“God, what an absolute disgrace,” blogger Rustem Adagamov wrote, pointing out that the International Criminal Court had issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu and that the prime minister faces corruption charges in Israel.Adagamov stressed that Makarevich had “spent years condemning the crimes of Putin’s regime, Russian aggression, and the killing of civilians,” but was now “having a friendly chat with a politician accused of extremely serious international crimes,” helping him “build a favorable public image.” “This isn’t about principles anymore — it’s hypocrisy and double standards,” the blogger wrote.Some users on Facebook, where Makarevich’s conversation with Netanyahu has drawn the most discussion, supported the musician, saying that “everyone has the right to freedom of speech and freedom of choice.”Makarevich responded to the comments:Once again, my opponents have proved that their emotions run about a hundred times stronger than their brains — assuming they have any — and that they can outdo even the worst Kremlin trolls when it comes to being obnoxious. Pretty much what I expected. Building politics in our country around those attitudes is a bad idea. Take my word for it. I reserve the right to think what I think and say what I say. Enjoy the elections.At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

sources.headline: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
sources.text: After three years of regional war, this is a battle Israel always knew was coming.The general election on Tuesday hangs over a country that's deeply divided and ready for a fight.Polls published on Friday put the governing coalition and the main opposition bloc almost neck-and-neck, with half a million first-time voters due to cast their ballot and some 70,000 Israelis reportedly flying in from abroad specifically to vote.On Saturday night, vast crowds of opposition voters gathered in central Tel Aviv to demand a change of government."We're optimistic," 21-year-old Omri told me. "I want peace, I want security, and I want to end corruption and get the religious fanatics out." This campaign has been energized by new tactics - including AI videos designed to grab the headlines - and also by a new face.Gadi Eisenkot is, perhaps, not the man you might expect to take on the flashy, aggressive, media-savvy brand of Israel's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.Relatively new to politics, with a working-class Moroccan background, Eisenkot is a former military chief of staff who is renowned for his calm manner and low-drama approach. He's been dubbed by some as a "non-politician".But he and his centrist Yashar party have regularly pipped Netanyahu and his Likud party to the top spot in recent polls, the last of which was published on Friday, in line with Israeli election law.Israeli politics is the art of coalition-building, rather than the task of any one party winning power, but with the predicted result too close to call, Eisenkot's rising profile has sharpened a race many Israelis already see as existential for the future of their country.I watched him slip past the cameras at a community centre for Ethiopian Jews in the city of Ramle last week, through a gaggle of security personnel and advisors.One of those who had come to hear him speak was David, a smartly dressed man in a freshly-pressed shirt and navy jacket, who said he had met Eisenkot before."He looks you in the eye, not like a leader looking down at someone," David told me. "And he listens. He's very sympathetic."Eisenkot's appeal is often put down to his personal manner and profile. A softly-spoken military man whose son was killed during the Gaza War, he has presented himself as coming "from the periphery", not from Israel's wealthy urban elite.His Moroccan background became election headlines earlier this month when a pro-Netanyahu speaker used a racist slur to refer to Eisenkot during a TV debate, referring to him as a Moroccan "monkey"."These elections are about many issues," Eisenkot told the crowd gathered at the Ramle community centre. "They are about security, economy, education...but primarily, they are about the identity of the State of Israel, and what kind of Israel we want to see. A Jewish state, a democratic state, a liberal, tolerant, egalitarian state."This is music to opposition ears, who say Benjamin Netanyahu's government is a threat to Israel's democracy, pointing to his efforts to curb the powers of the judicial system, and his refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks on the grounds that the country's Supreme Court would be biased against him.Eisenkot, along with other opposition leaders, has attempted to draw voters away from Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party by promising such a state inquiry, which a recent survey suggests is supported by more than 70% of Jewish Israelis.He has also vowed to enforce court rulings on drafting ultra-Orthodox Jews into national military service - another measure that is popular with right-wing voters and opposition alike.Benjamin Netanyahu has hit back with a campaign focused on Israel's security, and a core campaign slogan of "No Surrender".He has repeatedly cast his rivals as soft on security, playing on the fears of some right-wing voters that Jewish opposition parties might ally with Israel's Arab parties to secure a majority, and suggesting this could compromise national security.Around one-fifth of Israel's population is Arab - many of whom describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.These are the first elections since the 7 October attacks, in which Hamas-led gunmen stormed through Gaza's border fence, killing almost people and taking 251 hostage.It was Israel's worst security failure, but three years on its prime minister is again running for re-election as the only man who can keep Israel safe."If the army had woken him in time, it wouldn't have happened," Shlomi Bashar told me, one of several die-hard Netanyahu fans drinking in a basement café in Jerusalem's Mahane Yehuda market. "He does bear a certain responsibility, but after the 7 October, he changed the entire Middle East."Netanyahu has been hammering home the message that Israel's wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, in the years after the 7 October attacks, have reduced existential threats to the country."We need him to be re-elected so that he can finish this work," said Shlomi. "In my opinion, he is one of the best leaders in the world. Most of the world loves him and respects him, because he is a strong man and his ideas are correct."The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun."As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power."My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich."Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN."The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures.""We need a change - we can't live with this government anymore," Galia said. "And I'm not talking about security, I'm talking first about humanity."Having voted for centrist parties in the past, Galia says she's decided to vote for Eisenkot this time around, because "he's an ordinary guy and I hope he'll continue the way he's talking". Her son Gal said he was deciding between Eisenkot and the left-leaning Democrats party of Yair Golan, another former army general."I'm not naïve. I know there are a lot of more militant voices from young generations," he said. "I don't know if Eisenkot will be better than Golan in terms of security, but I think we have bigger problems: economics, social problems, education, health. We didn't get new neighbours on October 7 - it was a major event, but didn't change how we see ourselves."Threats to security versus threats to democracy - these are old political tramlines for Israeli voters, deepened by the 7 October attacks, and by four years of the most right-wing government in Israel's history.But on some of the biggest international concerns, the differences between government and opposition are not as wide as it might seem.Gadi Eisenkot has pledged to end Hamas rule of Gaza within 18 months, either through a US-led peace plan, or through "military and operational capabilities".All the main opposition leaders have voiced support for some form of Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, which has expanded massively under the current government and is illegal under international law. None have openly committed to the idea of full Palestinian statehood, something Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to block. Eisenkot has spoken about creating the conditions for "autonomy or state-minus" under ultimate Israeli security control.Tuesday's vote could well end in deadlock, with neither government nor opposition able to form a majority without the support of Arab parties, which polls project could win enough seats to be kingmakers. All but one of Israel's Jewish opposition parties have so far rejected working with either of the two Arab party blocs.With Benjamin Netanyahu ramping up warnings of fresh threats from Iran, opposition voices warning of potential disruption to the ballot, and Israeli rights activists warning of a further spike in violence by settlers in the occupied West Bank, political instability at home could leave Israelis facing both a fresh test of their democracy, and fresh security threats.

sources.headline: Why Israel's election is one of the most important in its history
sources.text: Israeli voters are preparing to head to the polls in an election some have described as the most consequential in the country's history. It's the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023. Tuesday's vote could see Benjamin Netanyahu's almost two-decade-long period of right-wing rule replaced by a more left-leaning government. Emerging as Netanyahu's main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff, who says the election is about Israel's identity as a liberal and tolerant democracy. Netanyahu has made security central to his campaign, warning that electing his rivals would risk making Israel less safe. Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports.

sources.headline: Gadi Eisenkot campaigns on Moroccan roots in challenge to Netanyahu
sources.text:
Ahead of Tuesday's elections, party advertisements greet people arriving by train to the outskirts of the western Israeli city of Sderot.
Campaign posters with various slogans promote the right-wing Likud and the far-right Otzma Yehudit parties. However, one poster is seen more than any others: that of the liberal Yashar party.
Its slogan, "Rosh Memshala Dialna," combines the terms "prime minister" in Hebrew and the words "of our own" in Moroccan Arabic.
And there is a good reason why Eisenkot's campaign in Sderot and other cities on Israel's sociopolitical periphery focuses on his Moroccan roots.
Eisenkot's Mizrahi background
Sderot — located in the Negev desert, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) to Tel Aviv's south and just a kilometer away from the Gaza border — is a city with a large Moroccan Jewish community. In recent decades, the city has become symbolic of Moroccan-Jewish culture in Israel, finding its expression in music, cinema and state politics. Israel elections: Who is Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's challenger?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Historically, Sderot is considered a bastion of the Israeli right, and especially a stronghold of Prime MinisterBenjamin Netanyahu's Likud. In 2022, Likud received more than 40% of the votes in Sderot, compared with 23% nationwide. Other members of Israel's far-right coalition received a lot of support there in the last election.
This pattern reflects deeper historical divisions in Israel between Ashkenazim, or Jews of European origin, and Mizrahim, or Jews mostly from Middle Eastern and North African backgrounds. According to estimates, half of Israel's Jewish population is of Mizrahi origin, amounting to about 4 million people.
Mizrahi Jews have faced discrimination and neglect since the early days of the Israeli state. This inequality still shapes the economic and social reality in Israel ― and its political discourse.
The issue has received special attention in the 2026 campaign. Eisenkot, Netanyahu's major challenger, is of Moroccan origin and grew up in Eilat, a city with a large North African Jewish population. Eisenkot's Yashar party accused Likud of sidelining its Mizrahi politicians. The campaign slogan, "Netanyahu: Let the Mizrahim give interviews,” mocked that omission. A sticker campaign in Sderot called for a Mizrahi prime ministerImage: Felix Tamsut/DW
On live television, the right-wing journalist Yinon Magal — one of Netanyahu's most vocal supporters — claimed that Eisenkot was being controlled by elitist Ashkenazim and called him a "monkey."
Netanyahu, who is of European origin, condemned the remark.
Morocco-born Daniel Ben-Simon, an award-winning Israeli journalist and a former member of parliament, told DW that Eisenkot's embrace of his roots might have been forced upon him by Magal's comments — but it has historical value nevertheless.
"People don't use terms like 'Dialna' with pride," Ben-Simon said, referring to Eisenkot's embrace of the Arabic term "of our own" in campaign posters. He said Israeli society had long tried to erase the Arab identities of North African Jews.
Eisenkot's embrace of his identity serves as a way of "leaving the frame" set by society. "By using such a term, you're creating a new identity: an Israeli-Moroccan identity," Ben-Simon said. "Eisenkot is the first to allow this double identity to be expressed and still feel at home."
Israel's historical divide
After Israel's founding, the ruling socialist party, Mapai, whose leadership was largely Ashkenazi, pursued discriminatory policies against Mizrahim. Mizrahim were often expected to "Europeanize” rather than preserve their own culture, heritage, or Arabic language. These inequalities also took a material form. In the state's early decades, while European immigrants often received better housing and jobs, many Jews from Arab-speaking countries were sent to Ma'abarot, or temporary transit camps, often in remote areas with little infrastructure. Many later became "development towns,” which remained underfunded compared with Israel's central regions. That in turn resulted in poverty. Sderot, in the south, is one of the best-known development towns.
For many Mizrahim, limited access to jobs, education and infrastructure symbolized long-standing exclusion by the Mapai establishment. Likud, founded as a right-wing alliance in 1973, used this frustration effectively under Menachem Begin. Mizrahi support for Begin helped produce the Mahapach, or upheaval, when Likud first defeated the socialist camp and took power. Since then, Mizrahim have often been associated with Likud, even though the party has never had a Mizrahi leader.Sderot's changing demographics
Over the past two decades, Sderot's proximity to Gaza has made the city a frequent target of rocket attacks launched by the militant group Hamas. During the Hamas-led terrorist attacks on October 7, 2023, the city of Sderot was hit especially hard. More than 50 people were killed. In the three years since the attack, the city's population has grown by about 5,000 people, bringing it to 40,000, with many young families making the town their home, both as a result of idealism and government benefits.The Sderot memorial for the victims of October 7Image: Felix Tamsut/DW
Walking around the town, it's hard not to notice that the so-called national-religious community is becoming increasingly dominant. This community tends to vote for Bezalel Smotrich's far-right Religious Zionism party, a main member of Netanyahu's coalition. Though votes for Smotrich and his party are de facto votes for Netanyahu's bloc, the prime minister's Likud party itself could suffer losses in Sderot.
Regardless of the election's results, the perception of Sderot as a city of Moroccan Jews is not bound to change anytime soon. Ben-Simon said Eisenkot's election could serve as an opportunity for reshaping Moroccan Jews' future identity in Israel.
"The connection cities like Sderot have to their Moroccan roots would grow stronger as a result of an Eisenkot win," Ben-Simon said.
